hints: At the interior maximum $x=p$, the derivative of $y=x^3\cos(2x)$ is zero.
Differentiate with the product and chain rules, then factor out the non-zero power of $p$.
Use $0<p<\pi/4$ to apply the inverse tangent on the correct branch and obtain the stated fixed-point form.
walkthrough:
Differentiate $y = x^3\cos(2x)$ with respect to $x$ using the product rule $(uv)' = u'v + uv'$:
$$u = x^3 \implies \dfrac{\mathrm{d}u}{\mathrm{d}x} = 3x^2$$
$$v = \cos(2x) \implies \dfrac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x} = -2\sin(2x)$$
$$\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = 3x^2\cos(2x) + x^3(-2\sin(2x)) = 3x^2\cos(2x) - 2x^3\sin(2x)$$

Set the derivative equal to $0$ at the stationary point $x = p$:
$$3p^2\cos(2p) - 2p^3\sin(2p) = 0$$
$$p^2[3\cos(2p) - 2p\sin(2p)] = 0$$

Since $0 < p \leqslant \dfrac{\pi}{4}$, $p \neq 0$, divide by $p^2$ and isolate the trigonometric terms:
$$3\cos(2p) - 2p\sin(2p) = 0$$
$$2p\sin(2p) = 3\cos(2p)$$
$$\dfrac{\sin(2p)}{\cos(2p)} = \dfrac{3}{2p} \implies \tan(2p) = \dfrac{3}{2p}$$

Take the inverse tangent of both sides and solve for $p$:
$$2p = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3}{2p}\right)$$
$$p = \dfrac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3}{2p}\right)$$

hints: Turn the result from part (a) into a continuous root function, for example $f(p)=p-\frac12\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{3}{2p}\right)$.
Calculate $f(0.5)$ and $f(0.7)$, retaining enough digits to show their signs clearly.
Conclude from the sign change and continuity that a root, and hence the required $p$, lies between the two values.
walkthrough:
Define the continuous function $f(p) = p - \dfrac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3}{2p}\right)$ based on the equation $p = \dfrac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3}{2p}\right)$:
$$f(p) = p - \dfrac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3}{2p}\right)$$

State conclusion based on sign change and continuity:
$$\text{Since } f(0.5) < 0 \text{ and } f(0.7) > 0, \text{ and } f(p) \text{ is continuous on } [0.5, 0.7],$$
$$\text{by the intermediate value theorem there is a root } p \text{ between } 0.5 \text{ and } 0.7. \text{ Hence } 0.5 < p < 0.7.$$

hints: Use the fixed-point update $p_{n+1}=\frac12\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{3}{2p_n}\right)$, with angles in radians.
Take $p_1=0.5$, calculate $p_2$ from the given update, then feed each output back into the formula; record every iterate to 5 decimal places.
Continue until successive iterates agree sufficiently to justify rounding $p$ to 3 decimal places.
walkthrough:
Set up the iterative formula $p_{n+1} = \dfrac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3}{2p_n}\right)$ with starting value $p_0 = 0.5$ (working in radians):
$$p_1 = \dfrac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3}{2(0.5)}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}(3) = \dfrac{1.2490458}{2} = 0.62452$$

Round the converged value of $p$ to 3 decimal places:
$$\text{Since successive iterates round to } 0.596:$$
$$p = 0.596$$
